title: Well and Bell
premise: Ines Eastwick hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for twenty years the calls have come from listeners who died the week before—voices Ines has rationalized as grief, hoaxes, and bad phone lines. When a new digital recorder captures a second voice in Ines's own sleep recordings, answering questions Ines never asked aloud, they learn it is the Bellringer: a thing that keeps the town's dead singing a song whose final verse will bind them to it forever. To save the newest caller—a drowned girl named Wren—and themselves, Ines must recover the town's buried history of a lynching their own family helped conceal, learn the song's last verse without ever singing along, and ring the church bell backward at dawn. The ending: Ines sings the verse wrong on purpose, breaking the cycle but erasing every recording of the dead voices—including Wren's last goodbye—and chooses to stay visible at last, telling the truth on air about what the town did.
about_author: Marguerite Eastwick is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent a decade answering phones for strangers who couldn't sleep. They write horror about small towns, old debts, and the frequencies between stations.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. During another shift of Well and Bell, Ines takes a call from Wren, a girl who drowned three days ago, and for the first time the voice names things only the real Wren knew. Ines's careful explanations begin to crack as the switchboard lights up with the week's dead. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into reluctant belief—the safe distance of twenty years collapsing in one night.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, intercut with transcribed sleep recordings. Reviewing the tapes, Ines hears a low second voice answering questions asked in Ines's own sleep-slurred speech; it calls itself the Bellringer and says the song is nearly finished. Researching the station archives, Ines finds every prior host quit or vanished after learning one more verse. Emotional beat: paranoia and complicity—invisibility was a choice, and it protected no one.

chapters.title: What the Town Buried
chapters.summary: Ines's POV with Wren's calls as counterpoint. Following the Bellringer's taunts, Ines uncovers an 1899 lynching covered up by the founding families—including the Eastwicks, whose bell foundry cast the church bell from melted chains. The dead aren't haunting the town; they're being held, verse by verse, as collateral for the families' silence. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into resolve—justice outside the law means doing what the law refused.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ines's POV, climaxing at dawn in the belfry. As the Bellringer forces the town's sleeping residents to hum the penultimate verse, Ines climbs to the bell, learns the final verse from Wren's fading voice, and sings it deliberately wrong while ringing the bell backward. The holding breaks; the dead go quiet forever, taking Wren's goodbye with them. Emotional beat: costly release—Ines loses the voices but gains a voice, broadcasting the town's true history as the sun rises.
